title: Mathematical regularity and usefulness coincide in living forms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Mathematical regularity and usefulness coincide in living forms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: What is most beautiful and regular in natural form, as in the bee's cell, is also found to be most useful and excellent.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Moreover the perfection of mathematical beauty is such (as Maclaurin learned of the bee), that whatsoever is most beautiful and regular is also found to be most useful and excellent.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), the Epilogue; topic “Mathematical law and beauty”. Scope: natural forms generally, exemplified by the honeycomb

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-epilogue-02: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.11

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Although honeycomb geometry and material efficiency can be measured, their coincidence with beauty is not an empirical law without an external aesthetic metric. The universal evaluative claim is therefore not resolvable as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Beauty, regularity, usefulness and excellence lack independent objective definitions here, so no non-circular dataset analysis supplies a confirming or refuting criterion.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Beauty and excellence are evaluative terms.

The scope and comparison class are unrestricted.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.12
discriminating power: 0.05
analysis feasibility: 0.2
data adequacy: 0.05

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The epilogue asserts a general coincidence of mathematical beauty and usefulness, with the bee's cell as an illustration. Usefulness can be defined for particular structures. The universal identification of the most beautiful with the most useful has no measurable contrast that would refute it.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The claim identifies whatever is most beautiful and regular in natural form with whatever is most useful. Beauty and regularity are not fixed measured variables, so no dataset can show that the most regular forms are the most useful across nature generally.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: A special case such as the honeycomb can be studied mechanically without giving the universal wording a decision criterion.
